title: Describe the API contract as a machine-readable manifest
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing visible. Today the only description of what the screens expect from a backend is TypeScript that a Go program cannot read, so a real backend that misspells or forgets a field would show up as a blank on screen, or as a total that is silently missing a part. After this lands that description also exists as a file both sides read, and the gate can catch the mismatch before anyone sees it.

## Outcome
Every method of the interface's API contract is classified, and one generated, versioned file describes the whole contract for a non-TypeScript reader: each method's route, class, argument schemas and result schema, plus the error envelope. The gate fails when that file is stale.

## Context
The interface talks to its backend through one TypeScript interface, `FinwiseApi` in `web/src/api/types.ts`, with 13 domains and 82 methods declared in `web/src/api/contract/`. Today an in-memory stand-in (`web/src/api/fake/`) implements it. A Go backend is being built to implement the same contract; it will be read-only at first: reads answer, every write is refused with one error.

**Why a classification.** Nothing in the types says which methods change state. The server needs that to refuse writes without a handler per write, and tests need it to prove none was forgotten. Four classes:
- `session`: the PIN gate itself, `session.status`, `session.unlock` and `session.lock`.
- `read`: returns data and changes nothing.
- `evaluate`: takes a draft, computes a result and stores nothing (`budget.evaluateScenario`).
- `write`: changes state. `session.changePin` and `changes.undo` are writes.

The classification lives beside the contract as a constant checked by a mapped type over `FinwiseApi`, so a method that is added, removed or renamed without being classified is a type error, not a runtime surprise.

**Why an error type.** The contract has none: failures are `null`, a result union for the PIN, or prose comments saying "Refused". A backend that refuses writes needs one representation. Kinds: `locked` (no valid session), `read_only` (a write or an evaluation was refused), `ledger_unavailable` (the bank data cannot be read), `bad_request`, `unknown_method`, `internal`, and `network` (client side only: the request never got an answer). On the wire an error is `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>"}}`.

**The wire, decided.** One route per method, `POST /api/<domain>/<method>`, whose body is the JSON array of the method's arguments in declaration order and whose answer is the method's result as JSON (`null` for a method that returns nothing). An optional trailing argument may be omitted or `null`. Rejected: resource-style REST, which needs 82 hand-written mappings on each side for no other consumer.

**The manifest.** A script under `web/scripts/` writes `internal/contract/contract.json` with: a format version; for every method its domain, name, route, class, an array schema for its arguments and a schema for its result; the shared definitions; and the schema of the error envelope. Object schemas forbid properties the contract does not declare. The file is versioned and never edited by hand, like `web/src/styles/tokens.css`; the freshness check compares the generated output with the file on disk, not with git, because a built but uncommitted change must not fail the gate that runs before the commit.

**The generator and its risk.** `ts-json-schema-generator` 2.10.0 (MIT, supports TypeScript from 5.9 below 7; the repository is on 6.0.3) is the first choice. It may not resolve a mapped or conditional type that extracts arguments and results from `FinwiseApi`. Settle that first: if it cannot, walk the methods with the TypeScript compiler API, which is already a dependency, and use the generator only for named types. Either way no schema may come out as the empty schema.

**Proving the schema can fail.** The stand-in is type-checked against the contract, so every answer it gives must validate. A test calls every `read` method of the stand-in over the prototype dataset and validates each answer against its result schema with `ajv`. If an answer does not validate the schema is wrong. The same test mutates one answer (a number turned into a string, a required field removed, an unknown field added) and expects each mutation to be rejected.

Dependencies are pinned to exact versions, as everywhere in `web/package.json`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Removing one method's entry from the classification makes `npm --prefix web run typecheck` fail, and so does adding an entry for a method that does not exist.
- [ ] `internal/contract/contract.json` lists every method of `FinwiseApi` exactly once, each with a route of the form `/api/<domain>/<method>`, a class, an arguments schema and a result schema.
- [ ] `session.status`, `session.unlock` and `session.lock` are `session`; `session.changePin` and `changes.undo` are `write`; `budget.evaluateScenario` is `evaluate`.
- [ ] No arguments schema and no result schema in the manifest is the empty schema or accepts any value.
- [ ] Every answer of every `read` method of the stand-in, over the prototype dataset, validates against its result schema.
- [ ] A number turned into a string, a required field removed and an unknown field added are each rejected by validation.
- [ ] `bin/ci` fails with a message naming the manifest when `contract.json` on disk differs from what the script generates, and passes after the script is run.
- [ ] `ApiError` and its kinds are exported from the contract, and the error envelope's schema is in the manifest.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and editing any contract type without regenerating the manifest makes it fail.

## Tests
- Unit: the manifest covers the classification one to one; route format; no empty schema.
- Conformance: every stand-in answer against its schema, and the three mutations rejected.
- Unit: the freshness check fails on a stale file and passes on a fresh one.
- The type-level guard is broken once on purpose and the compiler error quoted in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/errors.ts`, `web/src/api/types.ts`, `web/scripts/contract-manifest.mjs`, `web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts`, `web/package.json`, `web/package-lock.json`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `bin/ci`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/fake/`, `web/src/api/contract/`

Two new contract files, one script with its test, one generated file, and one new step in the gate. No screen, no store and no stand-in rule changes; `web/src/api/types.ts` only gains exports.
close_reason: Every method of FinwiseApi is classified under a mapped type (removing or inventing an entry fails typecheck with TS2741 / TS2353). internal/contract/contract.json lists 82 methods (3 session, 23 read, 1 evaluate, 55 write) with route, class, argument and result schemas and the error envelope; contract:check exits 1 on a stale file and bin/ci names the manifest. Every read answer of the stand-in validates with ajv and the three mutations are rejected. bin/ci: CI green. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%.

title: Work out the card's bills and each pot's balance and yield
description:
## What changes for the user
The card page has to answer three questions: when does the bill close, which bill is this purchase on, and how much of what was already spent this month will only be charged next month and has to be set aside. The pots page has to say how much each pot holds and how much it yielded this month. Today those answers come from invented constants. After this lands they can be worked out from the bank's own records, and where the records cannot support an answer the app says it does not know instead of showing a zero.

## Outcome
Two Go packages of pure functions: `internal/cardrules` (the closing date, the bill a purchase falls on, the amount that falls on the next bill) and `internal/potrules` (a pot's identity over time, its latest balance, its yield for a month with the daily rows behind it), plus the ledger query for a pot's yield.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app over a SQLite ledger collected from the person's banks. `internal/ledger` already reads that ledger read-only and returns typed rows with amounts in integer cents; `internal/brday` gives a day and a month in Brazil time. This bead adds interpretation for the card and for savings pots. Apart from the one query it adds to the reader, it does no SQL and no I/O.

**The closing date is predicted from a table, never read from a forecast.** The provider's `creditCardMetadata.billForecastDate` carries only a month on the card in use and must not be read. For that card (C6) the closing date depends only on the weekday of the nominal due date, with no exception across the bills examined:

| the due date falls on | days from closing to due |
| --- | --- |
| Monday to Thursday | 6 |
| Friday | 7 |
| Saturday | 7 |
| Sunday | 8 |

Which table applies to a card is the caller's choice: the rules take the table as a parameter and export the one above; this package does not work out which bank an account belongs to. The ledger keeps the nominal due date. The bank moves a due date on a non-business day to the next business day for payment, and that does not change the closing date. The due day itself is read from the ledger, never written in code. A card of a bank with no such table (the Itaú cards show no single offset per weekday) has an unknown closing date: return unknown, do not guess.

**`bills.closing_date` is the first day of the next cycle.** A purchase dated, in Brazil time, on or after a bill's `closing_date` belongs to the next bill; the day before belongs to that bill.

**The bill of a purchase.** `creditCardMetadata.billId`, when present, joins `bills.id` and is the answer. When absent, the purchase belongs to the first bill whose closing date is after the purchase day; with no such bill yet, to the predicted next one.

**The amount that falls on the next bill.** The purchases of the month dated on or after the predicted closing date, plus those of the two days before it that have not received the closed bill's `billId` (a purchase made right before closing sometimes slips to the following bill).

**A manual closing day** is a setting the person can choose later; the rules take it as an optional parameter, and it moves the closing date while the due date stays fixed.

**Pots.** `reserved_balance_history` has one row per reserve entry of an account's latest sighting of a day. A pot is identified by `reserve_id`, valid only when `stable_identity = 1`; names repeat, so two pots with one name are two pots. A pot whose identity is not stable cannot be followed across days and is reported for its latest day only. The latest balance comes from the reader's existing query. A pot absent from the latest sighting of its account is closed.

**Yield is not the change in balance.** A deposit raises the balance and yields nothing. The collector's README has a query for it, `caixinha_yield` (near lines 339-555 at the time of writing): copy it into the reader with a citation and honour its `reason` column, which says when the yield of a day cannot be computed. When it cannot, the yield is unknown, not zero. Decided with the user: yield is shown per month and opens to its daily rows.

**Two bases.** Nubank reports yield net of tax and Mercado Pago gross. Whether to convert to one base is open; until then every yield figure carries its base, and two bases are never added together.

**Attributing a movement to a pot.** A deposit or withdrawal row sits on the account and does not name the pot. This package receives such movements as plain values (account, day, amount) and attributes one to a pot when the account has exactly one pot, or when exactly one pot's balance changed by that amount on that day; otherwise the movement stays on the account as unattributed and is counted.

**What the sources leave open.** For each, write the smallest safe rule, state it in a comment, and report how many rows it matched on a real ledger, as a count only: the bill of a purchase with no `billId`; movement attribution; one base for yield.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] For a due date of 2026-01-12 (Monday) the closing date is 2026-01-06; 2026-03-12 (Thursday) gives 2026-03-06; 2026-06-12 (Friday) gives 2026-06-05; 2026-09-12 (Saturday) gives 2026-09-05; 2026-04-12 (Sunday) gives 2026-04-04.
- [ ] A card of a bank with no table returns an unknown closing date.
- [ ] A purchase on a bill's `closing_date` belongs to the next bill, and one the day before belongs to that bill.
- [ ] A purchase with a `billId` belongs to that bill even when its date says otherwise.
- [ ] A fixture carrying a `billForecastDate` that contradicts the table changes no result.
- [ ] The amount for the next bill includes a purchase on the predicted closing date, includes one made the day before without the closed bill's `billId`, and excludes one made the day before that carries it.
- [ ] A manual closing day moves the closing date and leaves the due date unchanged.
- [ ] Two pots with the same name on one account are two pots with separate balances.
- [ ] A pot with `stable_identity = 0` is reported for its latest day and has no history.
- [ ] A day with a deposit and no yield reports a yield of zero for that day, not the deposit.
- [ ] A day the query marks as not computable makes the month's yield unknown.
- [ ] Yields of a net pot and a gross pot are never summed into one figure: the function that totals yields returns one total per base.
- [ ] A movement on an account with one pot is attributed to it; on an account with two pots it is attributed only when exactly one pot's balance changed by that amount that day; otherwise it is returned as unattributed.
- [ ] The yield query is prepared against the collector's real schema by the existing schema test.
- [ ] A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs the rules over a real snapshot and logs only counts: bills, purchases per bill source (`billId` or date), pots, months with known and unknown yield, movements attributed and unattributed.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run completes with counts and no error.

## Tests
- Unit: the closing table for each weekday and for year and month ends; bill assignment on both sides of a closing date; the next-bill amount.
- Unit: pot identity, closed pots, yield against deposits, unknown yield, the two bases, movement attribution.
- Golden: the yield query against the real schema file.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each rule is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield_test.go`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `web/src/api/contract/card.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/savings-pots.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/card-rules.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/savings-rules.ts`, `bin/ci`

Two new packages of pure functions with their tests, and one new query in the reader: its statement joins the registry in `queries.go`, where a test requires every statement of the reader to live, and its code is a new file. No other reader file changes.
close_reason: internal/cardrules predicts a card's closing date from a weekday table passed in by the caller, places a purchase on its bill (the bill id wins; otherwise the first bill closing after the purchase day; unknown beyond the window or without a table), and sums what the month's spending puts on the next bill. internal/potrules follows a pot by its stable reserve id, reports a pot without one for its latest day only, gives a month's yield with its daily rows and its base, never adds two bases, and attributes a movement only when exactly one pot can claim it. The reader gains the collector's yield query, run as three statements over the same CTEs because the single statement does not prepare in this module's SQLite. bin/ci: CI green; the opt-in runs over a real snapshot completed with counts only. Review added a test for the closing day itself. Left for the reads: the yield query is slow when called once per pair of sightings, and a sighting with no pot returns no row.

title: Show a card's unknown closing date and next-bill amount as unknown
description:
## What changes for the user
The card page says when the bill closes, the best day to buy, and how much of this month's spending falls on the next bill. For a card whose bank has no known closing rule the app cannot work those out, and today it answers them as blanks and as `R$ 0,00`. A zero there reads as "nothing to set aside", which is not what is known. After this lands such a card shows a dash for each of them.

## Outcome
The card overview's closing date, best purchase day and next-bill amount can be unknown in the contract, the backend answers them as unknown for a card with no closing rule, and the card page and the home summary show a dash.

## Context
finwise's interface reaches its backend through a TypeScript contract (`web/src/api/contract/`), described for Go by a generated manifest that the gate keeps current (`npm --prefix web run contract`). The convention, stated in `AGENTS.md`: a field the ledger cannot always answer is nullable in the contract and a screen shows its absence, a dash for an unknown figure; a zero is for a figure that is truly zero.

The Go backend predicts a card's closing date from a table that depends on the bank (`internal/cardrules`). Only one bank has a table. For a card of any other bank the rules answer "unknown" for the closing date and for the amount that falls on the next bill. The contract's `CardOverview` cannot carry that: `closesOn` and `bestPurchaseDay` are required strings and `payAhead.amount` is a required number, so the handler in `internal/api/card.go` writes empty strings and 0. The card in use today belongs to the bank that has a table, so the case does not show on screen yet; it will the day the card in use is another bank's.

The home summary's pay-ahead is already nullable and is offered only when known.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] In the contract, `CardOverview.closesOn`, `CardOverview.bestPurchaseDay` and the pay-ahead amount of the card overview are nullable, and the manifest is regenerated.
- [ ] Over a fixture card of a bank with no closing table, `card.overview` answers `null` for the three, and still answers its due date, its limit and its past bills.
- [ ] The card page shows a dash for each of the three and no "R$ 0,00" for the next-bill amount; a test mounts it over the stand-in with such a card.
- [ ] Over the prototype dataset nothing changes: `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] The backend's golden files for the card are re-recorded from the fixture ledgers and its answers still validate against the schema.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, parity is unchanged, and a card with no closing table shows three dashes.

## Tests
- Unit: the handler over a card with no table.
- Component: the card page over the stand-in with unknown closing fields.
- Conformance: the stand-in's and the backend's card answers against the regenerated schema.
- Golden: the card overview's answers.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/card.ts`, `web/src/screens/contas/CardScreen.vue`, `web/src/api/fake/card-rules.ts`, `web/src/test/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/api/card.go`, `internal/api/card_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`
**Reads only:** `internal/cardrules/`, `web/src/lib/format.ts`, `AGENTS.md`, `bin/ci`

Three fields of one contract type become nullable, one screen and one handler follow, and the generated manifest and the card's golden files are refreshed.

title: Make every screen hold on a fresh install
description:
## What changes for the user
Every screen was built against a design that shows a year of use: a budget, subscriptions, months already closed, a chart with history. Nobody has seen the app on its first day, and a real backend that only reads the bank's records is exactly that first day. Today several screens would show `NaN`, a blank area or nothing at all. After this lands every screen opens cleanly both when the bank data exists and nothing else does, and when there is no data whatsoever: zero where zero is true, a dash where a figure is not known, a short sentence where a list is empty.

## Outcome
The in-memory stand-in can start in two new states, a fresh install with bank data and an empty ledger; the contract is nullable wherever a fresh install has no honest value; every screen renders both states without an error; and a test sweeps every route over both.

## Context
finwise's interface (`web/`, Vue 3) reaches its backend through a TypeScript contract, `FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/types.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/`). An in-memory stand-in (`web/src/api/fake/`) implements it over the design prototype's dataset, and `createFakeApi(options)` accepts a `state`. A real, read-only backend is being built: it will answer what the bank's records support and return everything the person authors inside the app (budget, budget lines on transactions, tags, nicknames, subscriptions, review marks, settings) as on a fresh install. The design prototype has no first-run screens, so those states were never built or measured.

A generated manifest, `internal/contract/contract.json`, carries a JSON Schema for every method's result, and an existing test validates the stand-in's answers against it. Changing a contract type means regenerating the manifest (the gate fails otherwise).

**Two states.**
- *Fresh install*: accounts, transactions, the card's bills, pots and investments exist; nothing the person authors does. Transactions have no budget line, no tag, no nickname and nobody classified them; pots have no bucket, no target and no linked line; there is no budget, no subscription, nothing to review, no closed month; settings are the defaults.
- *Empty ledger*: nothing at all, as before the first synchronisation. No account, no transaction, no card, no pot.

Both are built from invented data, like every fixture in the repository.

**Never invent a value.** Where the contract requires a field that has no honest value in one of these states, the field becomes nullable in the contract and the screen learns to show its absence. Known candidates, to be confirmed against the types: who classified a transaction when it has no line; the bucket of a pot and of an account; the card overview when there is no card; the last backup in the settings; the suggested threshold with no corrections behind it; the salary account's balance with no such account. A zero is used only where zero is the truth (a budget cap with no budget is 0). The full list of widened fields goes in the pull request.

**What the screens show.** Follow the vocabulary the interface already has: the empty block of the transaction list (`web/src/components/transactions/TransactionList.vue`) for an empty list, a dash for an unknown figure, `R$ 0,00` for a true zero. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese. No new visual component and no new token unless a state cannot be expressed without one; a color, size, radius, shadow or spacing step is never written as a literal.

**Known breaks.** `web/src/screens/patrimonio/chartGeometry.ts` divides by the chart's maximum with no guard for zero. `FakeState.card` is required, so a state with no card does not type-check. The Início, Budget, Patrimônio and card screens were partly read and assume their objects exist; Revisão, Cofrinhos, Assinaturas, Contas, Configuração and the transaction panel were not audited at all.

**The design does not move.** The prototype's dataset and every existing parity state stay as they are: the parity check must report the same result. The new states have no reference to be measured against, so they are covered by tests and looked at by a person.

**Looking at it.** The dev server starts the stand-in in one of the new states when `VITE_FINWISE_STATE` is `fresh` or `empty` (`VITE_FINWISE_STATE=fresh npm --prefix web run dev`); unset, it is the prototype's dataset as today, and the built interface never reads the variable. One screenshot per screen in each state, taken with the pinned Playwright against that dev server at the two parity viewports, is saved under the git-ignored `work/fresh-install/`.

Writes over the new states are out of scope; so is any change to how a write is called.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The stand-in exports a fresh-install state and an empty-ledger state, and `createFakeApi({ state })` runs on each.
- [ ] Every answer of every `read` method over each of the two states validates against its result schema in the manifest.
- [ ] A sweep test mounts every route of `web/src/router.ts`, plus the transaction panel, a pot's page, an account's page, the card page and a subscription's page where the state has one, over both states: no error is thrown, no promise rejection is left unhandled, and the rendered text contains none of `NaN`, `undefined`, `Infinity`, `null`, `Invalid Date`.
- [ ] The chart geometry returns a finite height when the maximum is 0.
- [ ] A transaction with no line renders its row and its panel; a pot with no bucket renders in the list and on its page; the card page renders with no card.
- [ ] An unknown figure renders as a dash and never as `R$ 0,00`; a test asserts it for at least the last backup and an unknown yield.
- [ ] The prototype dataset is unchanged, and `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] The manifest is regenerated and the gate's freshness check passes.
- [ ] No component gains a raw design value: `npm --prefix web run check:tokens` passes.
- [ ] `VITE_FINWISE_STATE=fresh` and `=empty` start the dev server's stand-in in those states; with the variable unset the prototype dataset is served, and the production build's output does not change with the variable set.
- [ ] One screenshot per screen for each state and each of the two parity viewports exists under `work/fresh-install/`, and the pull request lists every widened field with what its screen shows.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, parity is unchanged, and the sweep passes over both states.

## Tests
- Conformance: the stand-in's answers over both new states against the manifest's schemas.
- Component: the sweep over every route and both states.
- Unit: the chart geometry at zero; each widened field's rendering.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose (a `NaN` reintroduced, a required field restored) and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `web/src/screens/`, `web/src/components/`, `web/src/stores/`, `web/src/test/`, `web/src/main.ts`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `web/src/router.ts`, `web/scripts/parity/`, `design/`, `bin/ci`

Wide on purpose: the same defect, a screen that assumes a year of data, is spread over every screen, and each fix is a few lines. The contract types change only by becoming nullable, the stand-in gains two states and keeps its dataset, and no write call, no route and no reference screenshot is touched.
close_reason: The stand-in starts as a fresh install or an empty ledger, the contract is nullable wherever a first day has no honest value, every screen shows a dash for an unknown figure, R$ 0,00 for a true zero and a sentence for an empty list, and a sweep mounts every route over both states. VITE_FINWISE_STATE starts the dev server's stand-in in either state; the prototype build is identical with and without it. A fresh pot starts in the bucket its bank declares, so the net worth counts it from the first day. bin/ci: CI green, 877 tests. Parity on the merged tree: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. Every read answer over the three states validates against the regenerated manifest. 83 screenshots under work/fresh-install were looked at.

title: Read pluggy-sync's snapshot through typed read-only queries
description:
## What changes for the user
Today everything finwise shows is an invented dataset; none of it is the person's own money. This is the first piece that reads the real ledger the collector writes every night. Nothing looks different on screen once it lands, but the app gains a tested way to ask that ledger for accounts, transactions, card bills, savings pots, investments and the state of the last synchronisation, and it refuses a ledger whose format it does not know instead of showing wrong numbers.

## Outcome
A Go module at the repository root (`github.com/gabrielassisxyz/finwise`) with a package that opens pluggy-sync's snapshot file strictly read-only for each call, pins its schema version, and answers typed queries over the documented surface only. It ships with the fixture builder every later Go test uses, a test that prepares every query against the real schema, an opt-in test over a real snapshot that reports counts only, and the Go toolchain joined to the gate and to CI.

## Context
finwise has no backend yet. `web/` is a Vue interface running on an in-memory stand-in. The backend will be one Go binary; this bead starts it and contains no HTTP.

**The ledger.** pluggy-sync is the separate, public collector that pulls bank data into SQLite every night. Beside its live database it publishes `pluggy-snapshot.db`: a verified copy written to a temporary file and swapped in by an atomic rename, mode 0600, journal mode `delete`. A reader uses the snapshot and never the live file. Nothing promises what an open handle sees across a swap, so the reader opens read-only, runs its query and closes, on every call.

**Version.** `PRAGMA user_version` is 1 today. The collector promises nothing to readers about it, so the reader accepts exactly 1 and returns a typed error for anything else, before any query runs.

**Surface.** Only this is stable: the nine current-state tables (`items`, `accounts`, `transactions`, `bills`, `investments`, `investment_transactions`, `consents`, `identities`, `categories`), the views listed in pluggy-sync's README, `daily_sightings` (used by a README query) and `runs`. Anything else is internal to the collector and must not be queried.

**What exists now.** On every current-state table a row is current when `state = 'present' AND ambiguous_run IS NULL`.

**The clean list of transactions** is a README query, not a view: the predicate above, joined to `document_coverage` with `covered = 1`, minus every `PENDING` row whose id appears in `pending_posted_candidates.pending_id` (the collector's heuristic pairing of a pending row with the posted row that replaced it). Copy the query and cite the README lines in a comment beside it; the README of the checkout at dispatch has it near lines 287-296.

**Transactions.** Columns are `id, account_id, date, description, amount, currency, type, category, raw`. Everything else lives in the `raw` JSON: `status` (`PENDING` or `POSTED`), `operationType`, `amountInAccountCurrency`, `currencyCode`, `descriptionRaw`, `paymentData` (`paymentMethod`, and `payer` and `receiver`, each with `name` and `documentNumber.value`) and `creditCardMetadata` (`cardNumber`, `billId`, `installmentNumber`, `totalInstallments`, `purchaseDate`, `billForecastDate`, `feeType`, `payeeMCC`). The `merchant` column is null on every row. `date` is a UTC timestamp on every row.

**Accounts and bills.** `accounts.type` is `BANK` or `CREDIT`. A card's limit, available limit, closing and due dates are in `accounts.raw.creditData`. The bank behind an account is told by `accounts.name` or the first segment of `accounts.raw.bankData.transferNumber`; the connector name is the same for every bank. `bills` has `due_date`, `closing_date`, `total_amount`, `minimum_payment`.

**Pots.** `reserved_balance_history` has one row per reserve entry of an account's latest sighting of a day. A pot's key is `reserve_id`, valid only when `stable_identity = 1`; names repeat across pots. The latest balance of each pot is the README query `reserves_as_of` (near lines 239-258); nothing is carried forward from an earlier day.

**Investments.** `investment_history` has one row per investment per day with `amount_gross`, `taxes`, `taxes2`, `amount_net`, `rate`, `due_date`, `status`. `amountOriginal` is never summed.

**Synchronisation.** The last sync is `max(finished_at)` over `runs` with `outcome = 'complete'`; a later run may be `partial`. A connection is in trouble when `items.status != 'UPDATED'`, `execution_status != 'SUCCESS'`, or its last update is older than 48 hours. `consents.expires_at` and `revoked_at` are null in practice; the expiry is `items.raw.consentExpiresAt`.

**Money and days.** Amounts arrive as floating point out of JSON. The reader converts every amount to integer cents (round half away from zero) at its boundary, so no caller ever adds floats. A period is given in Brazil days and converted to UTC bounds inside the reader, because a row at 02:30 UTC on the 1st belongs to the last day of the previous month in America/Sao_Paulo.

**Scope.** The reader returns rows faithfully and interprets nothing: what kind a transaction is, the sign convention of the app, taxes folded into purchases and the card's bill rules belong to later beads. Its types must still carry every field named above, parsed, so those beads never touch SQL.

**Privacy, the rule above all others.** The ledger is a real person's complete financial history and this repository is public. A real snapshot may be opened read-only to check schema, JSON keys and counts. No value from it is ever printed, copied, logged, committed or pasted. Every fixture and every test uses invented literals.

**Decided, with what lost.** `modernc.org/sqlite` (pure Go, keeps one static binary) over the cgo driver. Reopening per call over a long-lived handle, because of the rename. Copying README queries with a citation over views added to the collector, which would change its schema version and need a release there; that is revisited once the queries have proven themselves.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `go test ./...` passes from the repository root with no environment variable set and writes nothing outside the tests' temporary directories.
- [ ] A fixture whose `user_version` is 2 yields the typed unsupported-version error from every query and no rows.
- [ ] The snapshot is opened read-only: a test attempts a write through the same open path and it fails, and the fixture file's SHA-256 is identical before and after running every query.
- [ ] A test replaces the fixture file by rename between two calls and the second call returns the new content.
- [ ] The clean list, over a fixture holding one row of each case (state not `present`, `ambiguous_run` set, not covered, `PENDING` with a posted pair, `PENDING` without a pair, `POSTED`), returns exactly the unpaired pending row, the posted row and the posted half of the pair.
- [ ] A transaction dated `2026-03-01T02:30:00Z` is returned for February 2026 and not for March 2026.
- [ ] `19.99` becomes 1999 cents, `-0.005` becomes -1, and a sum of one thousand rows of `0.10` is exactly 10000.
- [ ] The consent expiry is read from `items.raw.consentExpiresAt`; a fixture with `consents.expires_at` null and that key set returns the key's value.
- [ ] `internal/ledger/testdata/ledger-schema-v1.sql` is the collector's real schema, a test asserts it contains no `INSERT`, and a test prepares every query of the package against a database built from it. Renaming one selected column in any query makes that test fail.
- [ ] A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs every query over that file and logs row counts only.
- [ ] `bin/ci` runs `gofmt -l` (failing on any output), `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` and `go build ./...`, and still ends with `CI green.`; the workflow installs the Go version named in `go.mod`; every existing step is unchanged.
- [ ] `go.mod` requires `modernc.org/sqlite` and nothing else directly.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` describes the Go side under "Stack & Commands" and states the real-ledger rule under "Tests".
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` on the branch and the opt-in run over a real snapshot completes with counts and no error.

## Tests
- Unit: cents conversion and rounding; Brazil-day and month bounds, including the daylight-free UTC-3 offset at month and year ends.
- Unit over synthetic fixtures: one test per query, each asserting the exact rows returned for a fixture that also holds rows that must be excluded.
- Unit: version refusal, read-only open, file hash unchanged, rename between calls.
- Golden: the schema file against every prepared query.
- Integration, opt-in: the whole query set over a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `go.mod`, `go.sum`, `internal/ledger/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `bin/ci`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.gitignore`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/contract/`

Three small Go packages, all new: `internal/ledger` (the reader, its `ledgertest` fixture builder exported for other packages' tests, and its `testdata`), `internal/money` (integer cents) and `internal/brday` (a day and a month in Brazil time). The gate and the workflow gain Go steps and keep every existing one. Nothing under `web/` changes.
close_reason: internal/ledger opens the snapshot read-only on every call (mode=ro plus query_only), pins user_version 1 with a typed error, and answers accounts, the clean list, bills, pots, investments, identities and the sync state; internal/money holds integer cents and internal/brday gives Brazil days as UTC bounds. Every statement lives in one registry that a test prepares against the collector's real schema. bin/ci: CI green with the four Go steps. The opt-in run over a real snapshot completed with counts and no error. Correction to the bead text: the transactions table has no merchant column at all, rather than a column that is always null.

title: Use the read-only app at the desktop on the real ledger
description:
## What changes for the user
For the first time the person opens finwise and sees their own money in it, at their own desk, instead of a designer's example. Everything the app shows about the bank's records gets a first look from the only one who can tell whether it is right, before anything that changes data is designed on top of it.

## Outcome
The user has used the read-only app at the desktop on a copy of the real ledger, and what was wrong or surprising is written down as beads.

## Context
finwise's interface was ported from a design and measured against it pixel by pixel, on an invented dataset; no person has ever opened it. Its backend reads the bank's records through rules that turn raw rows into the list a person expects: signs, purchases abroad, tax rows folded under their purchase, transfers between own accounts set apart, savings-pot movements out of the general list, the card's closing date, each pot's yield. Several of those rules were written where the sources were silent, and each reports how many rows it matched; only the person can say whether the result is right.

The part of the app that stores what the person authors (budget, categorisation, tags, subscriptions, closing a month) has no plan yet. That plan is the next piece of work, and it starts from what this first use shows. One finding already waits for it: the bank's records carry no merchant on any row, so the establishment of a card purchase is derived from its text.

This check runs at the desktop on purpose. Packaging the app as one binary and putting it on the home server come after the write side, so that the deployment is designed once.

**How to run it.** With a copy of the collector's snapshot at hand:

```sh
go build -o finwise ./cmd/finwise
printf '%s' '<six digits>' | ./finwise hash-pin        # prints the hash
FINWISE_PIN_HASH='<the hash>' ./finwise serve --ledger <path to pluggy-snapshot.db> --dev-insecure-cookie
npm --prefix web run dev:backend                        # in another terminal
```

Then open the address the dev server prints and unlock with the PIN.

**What to look at.** Início for two or three different months: is every purchase there once, is a purchase abroad in reais with its tax under it, are transfers between own accounts set apart. Contas and one account's page. The card page: the closing date, the due date, the amount that falls on the next bill. Cofrinhos: balances and yield against the bank's app. Patrimônio: the total against the sum the person knows. Budget, Assinaturas, Revisão and Configuração open empty, and trying to change anything says the app is read-only.

**Rules to confirm while looking.** Each of these was written where the sources were silent, and only the person can say whether the result is right:
- A debit on a bank account whose text starts with the bank's bill-payment wording is the payment of the card bill, shown as a movement and not as spending.
- A credit on the card with no operation type whose text names a payment is also a bill payment. Without the rule it would read as income.
- A card credit carrying a refund, cancellation or return word is a refund.
- A tax row named after its purchase is folded under it when it is 3.5% of the purchase, on the same card, within 3 days.
- An explicit international tax row is folded under a purchase abroad only when that card has exactly one such purchase that day. The others stay listed on their own: look for them on the cards that are no longer in use, and say whether they should attach by another key.
- A handful of rows no rule recognises are listed as ordinary transactions under "Outros".
- A card purchase with no bill id is placed on the first bill that closes after it; on a card with no known closing rule its bill is unknown.
- A savings pot counts as reserved and an investment as invested in the net worth until a bucket can be assigned.
- A deposit or withdrawal is attached to a pot only when exactly one pot can claim it; with only a few weeks of nightly balances most past movements stay on the account.

No real amount, name or document from the ledger goes into a bead, a commit or a screenshot attached anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The user has unlocked the app at the desktop against a copy of the real ledger.
- [ ] The user has opened every screen in the list above.
- [ ] Each thing found wrong is a bead of its own, described without any real value.
- [ ] Done when: the user says the read-only app is good enough to plan the write side on.

## Tests
- Manual: the walk through the screens above, by the user.

## Blast radius
No file is edited. The check only reads: the built binary, a copy of the snapshot, and the interface in a browser.

title: Answer the monthly closing and the settings as a fresh install
description:
## What changes for the user
The monthly closing and the settings are the last two screens still answered by nothing. After this lands they open against the real backend the way they would on the day the app is first installed: a closing with every step still to do and nothing to review, and settings at their defaults, with what the bank's records do support (the card's bill and closing day, the last synchronisation, the connections, the pots) shown for real. With them every screen of the app has a real answer behind it.

## Outcome
The backend answers the last two read methods of the interface's contract, `review.closing` and `settings.overview`. With them every read of the contract has a handler, and the list of reads still waiting for one is gone.

## Context
finwise's read-only backend already answers every other read: the frame, the accounts, the transactions, the card, the pots, net worth, the home summary, the budget, the subscriptions, the weekly review and payday. Its HTTP package (`internal/api`) has handlers registered per contract method, a money type that encodes integer cents as an exact decimal, a conformance test that validates every answer against the method's schema in `internal/contract/contract.json` over two fixture ledgers, golden files, the choice of the card in use, each pot with the bucket its bank declares, and a test-side list of reads still without a handler. The backend has no database of its own: the part of the app that stores what the person authors has no reviewed plan yet, so what only that part will know comes back as on a fresh install. The contract is already nullable where a fresh install has no honest value, and the stand-in's fresh-install state in `web/src/api/fake/first-run-data.ts` shows what these two methods answer on a first day.

| method | answer |
| --- | --- |
| `review.closing` | the month, not closed, pending count 0, the card's real bill or `null`, the closing steps all not done, every list empty |
| `settings.overview` | the card's title, the default label, the default categorisation thresholds, the bank's closing day, the last synchronisation, no backup, the real connections, the real pots each in the bucket the pots answer already gives it and with no linked line, no establishments, no people |

**The closing steps.** `review.closing` lists the steps of closing a month. On a fresh install each exists and none is done: the list is the full set of `ClosingStepId` values in `web/src/api/contract/review-closing.ts`, in the order the stand-in gives them, not an empty array.

**The card and the pots are already chosen.** Which card account is "the card", its bill and its closing day, and each pot with its bucket, are worked out by the handlers of the card and the pots. Call what they use; do not choose a card or a bucket a second time.

**Defaults.** The categorisation threshold, the minimum of examples and the manual closing day have no decided default. Take the values the stand-in starts with in `web/src/api/fake/`, keep them in one place in Go, and list them in the report so the user can change them. The suggested threshold has no data behind it on a fresh install and is the contract's empty value.

**Money, messages, privacy.** As everywhere in this package: cents in, an exact decimal out; any string the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in the one messages file; no value from a real ledger is printed, logged or committed.

**What the first reads left in place.** `internal/api/bank.go` has `bankLabels(accounts)`, the one place that says which bank an account belongs to. `nowOf(ctx)` gives the injected clock in Brazil time. The conformance test validates the answer of every registered read handler over both fixture ledgers, and the golden test records them, once it knows the argument sets of a new method. `fixtures_test.go` builds the two fixture ledgers: extend them instead of building a third. Golden files are named as the README in `internal/api/testdata/golden/` says. `shell.overview` already reports the sync state. The opt-in test over a real ledger walks every registered handler and logs counts only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Both methods answer 200 with a valid session and their answers validate against their result schemas over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] `review.closing` lists every `ClosingStepId` exactly once, none done; a test fails when the contract gains a step the handler does not list.
- [ ] `review.closing` reports the same bill for the card as `card.overview` does over the fixture, and `null` over a ledger with no card.
- [ ] `settings.overview` reports the fixture's last complete run as the last synchronisation, one connection per fixture item, each fixture pot with the same bucket `savingsPots.list` gives it, and no backup.
- [ ] The defaults are defined once and a test reads them from that place.
- [ ] The list of reads without a handler is empty and removed, and the test that every `read` in the manifest has a handler stays.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and a POST to every `read` route of the manifest answers 200 or a contract-valid `null` over both fixture ledgers.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the closing steps against the contract's list; the defaults.
- Integration with `httptest`: every `read` route of the manifest through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler and test files in the HTTP package with their golden files, and the removal of the pending list. Existing handlers are called, not changed.

title: Let the interface talk to a real backend
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the interface can only run on the invented dataset bundled with it. After this lands the same interface, built for real use, talks to the backend: the PIN is checked by the server, the screens show what the server answers, and three things that used to fail silently now say something. Trying to change anything shows one message that the app is read-only for now and leaves the screen as it was. A session that expired brings back the PIN screen. A request that fails shows a message with a button to try again instead of a blank page.

## Outcome
An HTTP implementation of the interface's API contract beside the in-memory stand-in, chosen when the interface is built, and one place that turns every failure of the API into what the person sees.

## Context
finwise's interface reaches its backend through one TypeScript interface, `FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/types.ts`). `web/src/main.ts` provides an implementation with `app.provide(apiKey, createFakeApi())`, and everything else calls `useApi()` (`web/src/api/context.ts`). The only implementation is the in-memory stand-in under `web/src/api/fake/`, which serves the design prototype's dataset; the parity check that measures every screen against the design depends on that dataset.

A generated manifest, `internal/contract/contract.json`, lists every contract method with its route (`/api/<domain>/<method>`) and its class (`session`, `read`, `evaluate`, `write`). The contract also exports `ApiError` with a `kind`: `locked`, `read_only`, `ledger_unavailable`, `bad_request`, `unknown_method`, `internal`, and `network` for a request that got no answer. A Go backend serves those routes: `POST`, the body is the JSON array of the method's arguments in order, the answer is the result as JSON (`null` for nothing), an error is `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>"}}`, and the session is a cookie the server sets. That backend is read-only: every `write` and `evaluate` method answers `read_only`.

**The client.** Built by iterating the manifest, not as an open-ended proxy, so it has exactly the contract's methods and a call to a method that does not exist cannot become a request. Each method posts its arguments with `credentials: 'same-origin'`, returns the parsed result (`undefined` for a method that returns nothing), and throws `ApiError` with the kind the server sent, or `network` when `fetch` itself fails.

**Chosen at build time.** `vite build` produces the interface for real use, with the HTTP client. `vite build --mode prototype` produces it with the stand-in; the parity scripts build in that mode. `npm --prefix web run dev` keeps the stand-in, PIN `123456`. A new `dev:backend` script runs the dev server with the HTTP client and proxies `/api` to `127.0.0.1:8080`. The stand-in and its dataset are loaded with a dynamic import so they are not in the bundle for real use, and the gate proves it by searching the built files for a sentinel string that exists only in the prototype dataset.

**Why failures need one place.** Nothing in the interface handles a rejected call today. A write is called in seven different patterns (the transaction panel's `write`, `useLineChange`, `actOnSelection`, `useSettingsWrites`, the `announce` helpers of the review and the subscriptions, the closing actions and the budget save, and the PIN form), about sixty call sites, with no shared wrapper; a rejected write becomes an unhandled rejection and a rejected read leaves a blank screen. Rewriting those call sites belongs with the part of the app that will make writes real. Here one function receives every `ApiError`, wired to both `app.config.errorHandler` and the window's `unhandledrejection` event:
- `read_only`: one toast, "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.", and `useRevisionStore().bump()`, so every screen fetches again and shows the server's state instead of an optimistic one.
- `locked`: the session store becomes locked, which brings the PIN screen back.
- `ledger_unavailable`: a toast, "Dados do banco indisponíveis no momento.", with the action "Tentar de novo".
- anything else: a toast, "Não foi possível carregar os dados.", with the action "Tentar de novo".

"Tentar de novo" bumps the revision counter, which makes the screens fetch again. The toast is the existing one (`useOverlayStore().showToast(message, actions)`); the design has no error variant and none is added. An error that is not an `ApiError` is not swallowed.

**Tests at the right boundary.** The client's own tests stub `fetch`, which is its boundary. Tests of screens keep the repository's rule: the backend is faked with `createFakeApi`, here wrapped by a small test helper that makes every `write` and `evaluate` method of the classification reject with `read_only`, so each write pattern is exercised through a real screen.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The client exposes exactly the methods of the manifest, and each one posts to its route with a JSON array body and `credentials: 'same-origin'`.
- [ ] A 403 answer carrying `read_only` rejects with an `ApiError` of that kind; a rejected `fetch` rejects with kind `network`; a `null` answer to a method that returns nothing resolves to `undefined`.
- [ ] The files produced by `vite build` do not contain the prototype dataset's sentinel string, the files produced by `vite build --mode prototype` do, and `bin/ci` fails if the first ever does.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] For each of the seven write patterns, a refused write through a mounted screen shows exactly one toast with the read-only text, bumps the revision counter once, shows no undo toast, and leaves no unhandled rejection.
- [ ] A call rejected with `locked` shows the PIN screen.
- [ ] A read rejected with `ledger_unavailable` shows its toast, and its "Tentar de novo" makes the screen fetch again and render once the read succeeds.
- [ ] A thrown error that is not an `ApiError` still reaches the console and shows no toast.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run dev` unlocks with `123456` on the stand-in; `dev:backend` sends `/api` to `127.0.0.1:8080`.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` describes the two builds and the two dev scripts.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, parity is unchanged, and the seven refused-write tests pass.

## Tests
- Unit: the client against a stubbed `fetch`: routes, bodies, results, each error kind.
- Unit: the failure function for each kind, and for a non-API error.
- Component: one refused write per write pattern through a mounted screen; a locked answer; a failed read and its retry.
- Build check in the gate: the sentinel string absent from the bundle for real use.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/http/`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `web/src/main.ts`, `web/src/stores/session.ts`, `web/src/test/`, `web/vite.config.ts`, `web/package.json`, `web/scripts/parity/`, `bin/ci`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `web/src/stores/overlay.ts`, `web/src/stores/revision.ts`

A new client directory, one new module for failures, the provisioning line in `main.ts`, a lock entry point on the session store, a test helper, the build modes and the gate's bundle check. No screen component and no write call site is edited.
close_reason: web/src/api/http builds the client by iterating the manifest and posts each method to its route with same-origin credentials; the implementation is chosen by a build constant, and the gate proves the build for real use carries neither the stand-in nor the prototype dataset. One function wired to Vue's error handler and to unhandledrejection turns read_only into one toast and a revision bump, locked into the PIN screen, and any other failure into a toast with a retry; no write call site was edited. bin/ci: CI green, 839 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. Each of the seven write patterns has a refused-write test. Known and left: after a refused month close the closing step collapses, which needs an edit to that screen.

title: Compare smaller local models with the outside model for nightly categorisation
description:
## What changes for the user
Every night, the transactions that fixed rules cannot classify are sent to an outside provider's
model: their descriptions, amounts and counterpart names leave the home server, and each call is
billed. The user accepted that for now and asked to know whether a smaller model running at home
could do the same job. Once this lands they have that answer in numbers taken from their own
transactions: which home-run model came closest, how far it trails or beats the outside one, and
whether switching would mean correcting more transactions by hand.

## Outcome
A committed report compares at least three models that run on the user's own hardware against the
outside model on the same set of transactions the user has already confirmed or corrected, and
ends with one recommendation: switch, keep the outside model, or send only the uncertain rows
outside.

## Context
The app assigns each transaction to a budget line, which is one row of the user's monthly budget
(groceries, transport and so on). Fixed rules do most of it: a company that always lands on the
same line is mapped once. What the rules cannot place goes to a language model in a nightly job
that runs with nobody present. The model's answer is applied by itself only when its confidence
is at or above a threshold the user sets, called the auto-apply threshold here; below it the
transaction waits in a queue for the user to decide.

It was decided that the backend reaches the model by calling an HTTP API directly, in the chat
format that outside providers and local model runtimes both accept, so that changing model is a
matter of two configuration values, the base URL and the model name. This bead is the test of
that claim as much as of the models: if a local model needs a different request, the claim is
false and the report must say so.

The user's words when asking for this: outside providers are fine "por enquanto", with a bead to
"avaliar/testar modelos locais menores". Privacy is one reason and cost the other. One guard
already holds on every path: a personal tax number (CPF) is never part of a request, because it
does not help classification.

Two constraints shape the work and are easy to break by accident:

- **The repository is public and the evaluation set is real financial data.** The labelled set
  and every per-row output stay outside the repository, in a directory git ignores. The report
  publishes aggregates only: no description, no counterpart name, no amount per row. Test
  fixtures are synthetic.
- **Which models to try is decided when the work runs, not here.** The set of small models that
  are worth trying changes from month to month, so naming them now would date the bead. The
  criteria fix how many and how they are compared instead.

The evaluation tool may be a script outside the backend, in Python, since it is run by hand a few
times and never deployed. The user was told this and did not object. It must send the same
request the nightly job sends, which is why this bead cannot start before that job exists.

It cannot start yet for a second reason: there is nothing to evaluate against until the user has
used the app long enough to confirm or correct a few hundred categorisations. Both waits are on
work that has no bead at the time of writing, so the bead is parked as blocked with a comment, to
be replaced by dependency edges when the categorisation work is written up.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The evaluation set holds at least 300 transactions whose budget line the user confirmed or
      corrected, spanning at least 3 calendar months, with every CPF removed. The report states
      its size and month span.
- [ ] At least 3 models running on the user's own hardware are measured, at no fewer than 2
      different sizes, beside the outside model in use on that day as the baseline. The report
      names each one with the exact version or tag that was run.
- [ ] Every arm receives the request the nightly job builds, byte for byte except the base URL
      and the model name. The report states this, or lists each difference a model required.
- [ ] For each arm the report gives four figures over the whole set: the share of rows whose
      budget line matches the user's; the share of rows answered at or above the auto-apply
      threshold in force (coverage); the share of matches among those rows; and the share of
      answers that were not valid against the response schema.
- [ ] For each local arm the report records the host's CPU, memory and GPU, and the peak memory
      the model used.
- [ ] Seconds per nightly batch, median of three runs per arm with the arms interleaved, are
      measured **by the review** rather than by whoever implements this, and recorded in the
      report.
- [ ] No file under version control contains a transaction description, a counterpart name or a
      per-row amount from the evaluation set: `git grep` for three descriptions sampled from the
      set returns nothing.
- [ ] The report ends with exactly one recommendation (switch, keep, or route by confidence) and
      the two figures it rests on.
- [ ] Done when: the report is committed at `docs/evaluations/local-models.md` and a reader can
      tell from it alone, without rerunning anything, which local model did best and by how many
      percentage points it trails or beats the baseline at the threshold in force.

## Tests
- Unit: the scoring functions (match share, coverage, match share above the threshold, invalid
  answer share) over a synthetic labelled fixture with known expected values, including a row
  with an invalid answer and a row exactly at the threshold.
- Unit: the loader refuses a set that still carries a CPF-shaped value.
- Manual check: the three measured runs per arm, standing in for an end-to-end test that cannot

## Blast radius

A new, self-contained tool directory (the script, its scoring module and their tests) and one
