title: Answer the budget, the subscriptions, the weekly review and payday as a fresh install
description:
## What changes for the user
Budget, subscriptions and the reviews are things the person builds inside the app, and the app cannot store anything yet. After this lands the Budget and Assinaturas screens, the weekly review and the payday review open against the real backend the way they would on the day the app is first installed: an empty budget, no subscriptions, nothing waiting for review, and the one figure the bank's records do support, the balance of the account the salary lands on, shown for real. Trying to edit a budget answers that the app is read-only for now.

## Outcome
The backend answers ten more read methods of the interface's contract: the four of `budget`, the four of `subscriptions`, `review.weekly` and `review.payday`.

## Context
finwise's read-only backend already answers the frame, the accounts and the transactions from the ledger. Its HTTP package (`internal/api`) has handlers registered per contract method, a money type that encodes integer cents as an exact decimal, a conformance test that validates every answer against the method's schema in `internal/contract/contract.json` over two fixture ledgers, golden files, and a test-side list of reads still without a handler. The backend has no database of its own: the part of the app that stores what the person authors has no reviewed plan yet, so what only that part will know comes back as on a fresh install. The contract is already nullable where a fresh install has no honest value, and the stand-in's fresh-install state in `web/src/api/fake/first-run-data.ts` shows what each of these methods answers on a first day.

| method | answer |
| --- | --- |
| `budget.document` | the budget's authored groups, each with no line, exactly as the stand-in's fresh-install state gives them |
| `budget.view` | the month, not closed, income 0, allocated 0, an unknown investment rate, and the same groups plus the derived ones, zero wherever the figure comes from the budget; the fees subtotal is the month's real fees |
| `budget.establishments`, `budget.scenarios` | `[]` |
| `subscriptions.list` | totals 0, no groups, no suggestion |
| `subscriptions.detail` | `null` |
| `subscriptions.candidates`, `subscriptions.recurring` | `[]` |
| `review.weekly` | the limit with cap 0 and spent 0 (the contract's "spent" is what was spent on the budget's variable lines, and there are none); no week, an empty queue, no approvals, no warnings |
| `review.payday` | the real balance of the account the salary lands on and its label, a cushion of 0, no transfers; the comparison with the cushion as the contract's fresh-install value |

**A budget draft is refused.** `budget.view` takes an optional draft and then evaluates it; that is the budget's arithmetic, which belongs to the part of the app not built yet. With a draft that is not `null` the method answers the `read_only` error, the same one every write answers. Without a draft it answers the table's row.

**Recurring purchases and subscription candidates** could in principle be detected from the ledger. Detecting them is not decided and belongs with the write side; they are empty here on purpose.

**An empty budget still has its groups.** The Budget screen draws its first-day state from the groups the API returns, so an answer with no groups would leave a blank area. The stand-in's fresh-install state is the reference for both budget reads, field by field. The one derived figure the bank's records support is the fees subtotal, taken from the month's listed transactions that the transaction rules flag as a fee, read through the same widened period the transaction list uses.

**The account the salary lands on.** The contract's payday figures use one account and the ledger has several. It is the bank account with the latest settled credit whose `operationType` is `FOLHA_PAGAMENTO`: a salary can move to another account, and the latest one is where it lands now. A real ledger was found to hold two accounts with such credits, an older one with many and a newer one with few, which is what a change of account looks like. The check over a real ledger asserts that the latest credit does not tie between two accounts and reports, as a count, how many accounts ever received one. With none, the balance and its label are the contract's empty value, and so is the comparison with the cushion: with no cushion set there is nothing to be above or below.

**Work in parallel.** Another change is adding the card, the pots, net worth and the home summary to the same package at the same time. Keep to files of your own, add one line per domain to the registration list, extend the shared fixture ledgers only by adding to them, and take from the pending list exactly the ten names of this bead.

**Money, messages, privacy.** As everywhere in this package: cents in, an exact decimal out; any string the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in the one messages file; no value from a real ledger is printed, logged or committed.

**What the first reads left in place.** `internal/api/bank.go` has `bankLabels(accounts)`, the one place that says which bank an account belongs to: use it wherever the bank matters and write no second one. `nowOf(ctx)` gives the injected clock in Brazil time. The conformance test validates the answer of every registered read handler over both fixture ledgers, and the golden test records them, once it knows the argument sets of a new method. `fixtures_test.go` builds the two fixture ledgers. Golden files are named as the README in `internal/api/testdata/golden/` says. The opt-in test over a real ledger walks every registered handler and logs counts only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the ten methods answers 200 with a valid session and its answer validates against its result schema over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] `budget.view` with a draft of `[]` answers 403 `read_only`; with no draft and with `null` it answers the empty view.
- [ ] `review.weekly` reports a limit of cap 0 and spent 0 over a fixture month that has purchases.
- [ ] `review.payday` reports the balance of the fixture account that received the latest `FOLHA_PAGAMENTO` credit, and the contract's empty value over a ledger with no such credit.
- [ ] `subscriptions.detail` answers `null` for any id.
- [ ] The pending list of reads without a handler no longer names these ten methods.
- [ ] `budget.document` and `budget.view` answer the same groups, in the same order, as the stand-in's fresh-install state, and over a fixture month with a fee the fees subtotal is that fee.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer, asserts that the latest payroll credit is not tied between two accounts, and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and each of the ten routes answers 200 or a contract-valid `null` over both fixture ledgers.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the draft refusal; the choice of the salary account.
- Integration with `httptest`: each of the ten routes through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `internal/txrules/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler and test files in the HTTP package with their golden files, one line per domain in the registration list, and ten names fewer in the pending list. Existing handlers are called, not changed.
close_reason: The backend answers the four budget reads, the four subscription reads, review.weekly and review.payday. An empty budget answers the stand-in's groups, with the fees subtotal taken from the month's real fees through the same widened read the transaction list uses; a budget draft answers read_only through the path a refused write uses. The payday shows the balance of the bank account with the latest settled payroll credit, and no comparison with a cushion that is not set. Every answer validates against its schema over both fixture ledgers and is recorded as a golden file. bin/ci: CI green. Over a real snapshot every answer validated and the latest payroll credit is not tied between accounts; two accounts were found to have received payroll, which is why the check no longer demands one.

title: Answer the card, the pots, net worth and the home summary from the ledger
description:
## What changes for the user
After the accounts and the transactions, the rest of what the bank's records can answer becomes real: the card page with its open bill, its closing and due dates and how much of this month's spending falls on the next bill; the savings pots with what each holds and what it yielded; net worth and its history; and the summary at the top of the home screen. Where the records cannot support a figure the screen says it is not known, and nothing that needs a budget pretends to have one.

## Outcome
The backend answers five more methods of the interface's contract from the ledger: `card.overview`, `savingsPots.list`, `savingsPots.detail`, `netWorth.overview` and `home.summary`, each checked against the contract's schema and recorded as golden files from invented data.

## Context
finwise's read-only backend already answers the frame, the accounts and the transactions. Its HTTP package (`internal/api`) has the machinery this bead reuses: handlers registered per contract method, a money type that encodes integer cents as an exact decimal, a conformance test that validates every answer against the method's schema in `internal/contract/contract.json` over two fixture ledgers (one with every shape, one empty), golden files, and an opt-in test over a real ledger that logs counts only. `internal/cardrules` predicts the card's closing date, places a purchase on its bill and computes the amount that falls on the next bill; `internal/potrules` gives each pot's identity, latest balance and monthly yield, and attributes movements to pots.

**Same rule as before.** A figure the ledger supports is real; anything only the person can author is the contract's empty value; nothing is invented. The contract is already nullable where a fresh install has no honest value.

**Which card.** The contract models one card; the ledger may hold several card accounts, and the interview with the user says one card is in use. A bank keeps issuing bills for a card nobody uses, so a recent bill does not tell which card is in use. "The card" is the card account with the most recent purchase; ties go to the later bill by due date, then to the account id; when no card account has a purchase it is the one with the latest bill. A real ledger was found with several card accounts that still receive bills and only one with purchases. An opt-in check over a real ledger asserts that exactly one card account has a purchase in the last 60 days; when it finds another number the work stops and the count is reported. With no card account at all, `card.overview` answers the contract empty value. The other card accounts are reachable as accounts.

| method | from the ledger | empty for now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `card.overview` | the open bill, when it closes and falls due, the best day to buy, the limit and what is left of it, the amount that falls on the next bill with its purchases, past bills | the card's label is the default; the closing mode is the bank's |
| `savingsPots.list`, `savingsPots.detail` | each pot's name as the bank gives it, balance, movements, the month's yield with its daily rows and its base (net or gross); closed pots when asked | target, planned contribution, linked budget lines; the bucket is the default below |
| `netWorth.overview` | the total, what is available, reserved and invested, the chart from the first month the ledger has a reading for, the pots' yields | planned contribution and planned investment rate 0 |
| `home.summary` | net worth's three parts, the amount that falls on the next bill | the limit is cap 0 and spent 0 (the contract's "spent" is what was spent on the budget's variable lines, and there are none), weeks `[]`, pending count 0 |

**Net worth.** Available is the balance of the bank accounts; reserved is the pots; invested is the investments at their net amount (`amount_net` of the latest day; `amountOriginal` is never summed). The stand-in's rules in `web/src/api/fake/` state how the three parts and the total relate; follow them. The balance history has one reading per night and starts recently, so the chart starts at the first month with a reading: a month before it is absent, never zero.

**A pot's bucket, decided with the user.** The person assigns each pot to a bucket (`Disponível`, `Reservado`, `Investido`), and nothing can be assigned yet. A pot counted in no bucket would be missing from the net worth, so until the person says otherwise the bucket is what the bank says the pot is: a reserve entry (a "caixinha") is `Reservado` and an investment is `Investido`. Bank accounts are available. The stand-in's fresh-install state follows the same rule. Rejected: counting an unassigned pot nowhere, which understates the total for as long as nothing can be assigned; and a fourth "no bucket" group, which adds interface outside the design for a state that ends when assignment exists.

**The same money must not be counted twice.** Some banks back a pot with investments, so one sum can appear both as a reserve entry and among the investments. The sources do not say how those investments divide between the pots. Count the reserve entries; leave out an investment only when the ledger itself shows it backs a reserve; otherwise keep both and report, as a count, how many investments sit on an account that also has reserve entries, so the case is seen and decided rather than guessed.

**Yield.** A month whose yield cannot be computed is unknown, not zero. Two bases are never added into one figure.

**What the card and pot rules expect of their caller.**
- `cardrules.Card` is built by the caller from the card account's bills, the closing table and an optional manual closing day. The rules do not know which bank a card belongs to: the caller picks `cardrules.C6ClosingTable()` for a C6 card and no table for any other, using the bank identification that `internal/txrules` already has. A card with no table has an unknown closing date and an unknown next-bill amount, and both reach the screen as unknown.
- `Card.AmountOnNextBill` sums the purchases it is handed with the sign they carry. Hand it the listed card purchases of `internal/txrules` (negative for money out) and present the figure as the contract expects.
- A pot's yield comes from `ledger.PotYields` between two days and `potrules.YieldOfMonth`, which needs the pot's base: net for Nubank, gross for Mercado Pago, by the account's bank. `MonthYield.Since` precedes the month when the account was not sighted on the days before; the total then holds yield earned before the month began, and the pot's page says since when.
- The yield statement of the collector's README does not prepare as one statement in this module's SQLite and runs as three statements over the same CTEs. Asking it once per pair of consecutive sightings took about 70 seconds over a real ledger. A request must not do that: ask for the range the screen needs in as few calls as the query allows, and measure.
- `potrules` attributes a deposit or a withdrawal to a pot only when a sighting within three days after it shows exactly one pot whose balance moved by that amount. The balance history is one reading per night and starts recently, so most past movements stay unattributed on their account. They are shown on the account's side of the pots screen as the contract allows, never dropped and never guessed onto a pot.
- `ledger.Pots` returns no row for a sighting in which the account holds no pot, so an account that emptied every pot does not make them read as closed. If the pots screen needs that case, the reader gains it here, with a test.

**Money, messages, privacy.** As everywhere in this package: cents in, an exact decimal out; any string the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in the one messages file; no value from a real ledger is printed, logged or committed, and golden files come only from the fixture builder.

**What the first reads left in place.** `internal/api/bank.go` has `bankLabels(accounts)`, the one place that says which bank an account belongs to: use it wherever the bank matters and write no second one. `nowOf(ctx)` gives the injected clock in Brazil time. The conformance test validates the answer of every registered read handler over both fixture ledgers, and the golden test records them, once it knows the argument sets of a new method. `fixtures_test.go` builds the two fixture ledgers: extend them with what this bead needs instead of building a third. Golden files are named as the README in `internal/api/testdata/golden/` says. Strings a person reads live in the one messages file. `accounts.detail` already answers a bank account with the bucket `Disponível`, and `shell.overview` already reports the sync state. The opt-in test over a real ledger walks every registered handler and logs counts only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the five methods answers 200 with a valid session, and its answer validates against its result schema over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] Over a fixture with two card accounts, `card.overview` describes the one with the more recent purchase, even when the other has the later bill; with no purchase on either it describes the one with the later bill.
- [ ] Over the empty ledger `card.overview` answers the contract's empty value, the pot list is `[]`, and net worth is zero with an empty chart.
- [ ] A fixture purchase dated on the predicted closing date is among the purchases that fall on the next bill; one dated the day before with the closed bill's id is not.
- [ ] A fixture pot whose month has a day the yield query cannot compute reports an unknown yield for that month.
- [ ] A fixture with one net pot and one gross pot never yields a single summed figure.
- [ ] Net worth's total equals available plus reserved plus invested for the fixture, to the cent; a fixture reserve entry is counted in reserved and a fixture investment in invested, and each pot's answer names that bucket.
- [ ] The chart has no month before the fixture's first balance reading.
- [ ] `home.summary` reports a limit of cap 0 and spent 0 over a fixture month that has purchases, and its net worth equals what `netWorth.overview` reports for the same ledger.
- [ ] `savingsPots.list` omits a closed pot by default and includes it when asked.
- [ ] A fixture card of a bank with no closing table answers `card.overview` with an unknown closing date and an unknown next-bill amount, neither shown as zero.
- [ ] A fixture movement no pot can claim is present in the pots answer as unattributed on its account.
- [ ] `savingsPots.list` and `savingsPots.detail` each run the yield query a number of times that does not grow with the number of sightings in the range; a test counts the calls.
- [ ] The time `savingsPots.list` takes over a real ledger is measured **by the review**, not by the lane, three runs on a quiet machine, and recorded on the pull request.
- [ ] The pending list of reads without a handler no longer names these five methods.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer, asserts exactly one card account with a purchase in the last 60 days, and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports every answer valid and one card in use.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the choice of the card; net worth's parts and total; the chart's first month; unknown yield.
- Integration with `httptest`: each method through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`, `internal/ledger/`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/txrules/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler and test files in the HTTP package with their golden files, and new history queries in the reader (balances, reserves and investments per day), each as a new file with its test. Existing handlers are not changed.
close_reason: The backend answers card.overview, savingsPots.list, savingsPots.detail, netWorth.overview and home.summary from the ledger. The card in use is the card account with the most recent purchase. A reserve entry counts as reserved and an investment as invested; an investment is left out only when the ledger shows it backs the reserves. Yield is unknown rather than zero when it cannot be computed, and two bases are never summed. Every answer validates against its schema over both fixture ledgers and is recorded as a golden file. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main. Over a real snapshot every answer validated and exactly one card account has a purchase in the last 60 days. Measured by the review on the built server over a real ledger, three runs each: savingsPots.list, savingsPots.detail and netWorth.overview take 12 to 15 seconds because of the collector's yield statement; every other read is under 0.4 s. That, and the daily yield rows that are always empty, are carried by a follow-up bead; a card with no closing rule answering blanks and a zero is carried by another.

title: Serve the contract over HTTP behind the PIN and refuse every write
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the PIN screen guards nothing: the lock lives in the browser's memory and the data is an invented dataset bundled with the page. After this lands there is a real program to start, `finwise serve`, that keeps the person's data behind the six-digit PIN on the server side, locks for five minutes after three wrong attempts, and answers every attempt to change something with one clear refusal, because this first backend only reads.

## Outcome
A `finwise` binary with `serve` and `hash-pin`. Its HTTP server exposes one route per method of the interface's API contract, built from the contract's manifest: session methods work, every write and every evaluation is refused, reads are dispatched to handlers registered by later work, and nothing but the session's own two routes answers without a valid session.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app. Its interface (`web/`) talks to a backend through a TypeScript contract of 82 methods. A generated file, `internal/contract/contract.json`, describes that contract for Go: for every method its route (`/api/<domain>/<method>`), its class (`session`, `read`, `evaluate` or `write`), a schema for its arguments and one for its result, and the schema of the error envelope. The Go module and a read-only ledger reader (`internal/ledger`) already exist. This bead is the HTTP layer between them; the read handlers themselves come later.

**The wire.** Every method is `POST /api/<domain>/<method>`. The body is the JSON array of the method's arguments in declaration order; the answer is the method's result as JSON, `null` for a method that returns nothing. An error is `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>"}}`:

| kind | status | when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `locked` | 401 | no valid session |
| `read_only` | 403 | the method's class is `write` or `evaluate` |
| `ledger_unavailable` | 503 | the reader reports a missing or unreadable snapshot, or an unsupported version |
| `bad_request` | 400 | the body is not a JSON array the method accepts, the content type is not JSON, the body is over 1 MiB, or the verb is not POST |
| `unknown_method` | 404 | no such route under `/api/` |
| `internal` | 500 | anything else |

**Refusing writes without a handler per write.** The router is built from the manifest. A `write` or `evaluate` method is refused before its body is read, and no handler exists for it. The session check comes first: without a session a write answers `locked`, not `read_only`. `session.changePin` is a write and is refused without comparing any PIN. This backend is read-only on purpose: the part of the app that changes data has no reviewed plan yet.

**Reads.** A `read` method is served by a handler registered for it, receiving the request context, the raw arguments and a way to open the ledger. This bead registers none. A test holds the list of `read` methods still without a handler and fails when the manifest's reads differ from registered plus listed; later work empties that list. A `read` with no handler answers `internal`.

**The PIN.** One six-digit PIN, no user name. The server never stores it: it reads `FINWISE_PIN_HASH`, a string of the form `pbkdf2-sha256$<iterations>$<salt>$<key>` (base64 fields, at least 600000 iterations), derives the key from the attempt with the standard library's `crypto/pbkdf2` and compares in constant time. `finwise hash-pin` reads a PIN from standard input, refuses anything but six digits, and prints that string. `finwise serve` refuses to start when the variable is missing or malformed, and its message never contains the value. A six-digit PIN cannot be protected against someone who holds the hash; the hash keeps the PIN out of configuration in the clear, and the lockout protects against guessing over the network.

**Lockout.** Three wrong attempts lock every attempt out for 300 seconds, the right PIN included; a correct attempt resets the count. The lock is global, not per client: there is one user. `session.status` answers `{locked, retryAfterSeconds}` and `session.unlock` answers the contract's `UnlockResult` (see `web/src/api/contract/session.ts`). The in-memory stand-in in `web/src/api/fake/index.ts` is the statement of the same behaviour. The clock is injected so tests do not wait.

**Sessions.** A successful unlock creates a random 256-bit token kept in memory and sets a cookie named `__Host-finwise-session` with `Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` and no `Domain`. A session expires after 12 hours without a request (`FINWISE_SESSION_TTL` overrides it); the server decides expiry and the cookie lives at least as long. `session.lock` removes the session and clears the cookie. Sessions are lost when the process restarts, which only means typing the PIN again. A flag `--dev-insecure-cookie`, off by default, drops `Secure` and the `__Host-` prefix for a plain-HTTP development setup.

**Cross-origin.** Wrap the mux in the standard library's `http.CrossOriginProtection`, and require `Content-Type: application/json` on every `/api/` request.

**Logs.** `log/slog` to standard output: method, route, status, duration. Never a body, an argument, a cookie, the PIN, the hash, or a value from the ledger. The person's whole financial history passes through this process. An error returned by the ledger reader may carry a row id in its text: log the error's kind, never its message.

**Serving.** `finwise serve --listen <addr> --ledger <path>` (`FINWISE_LISTEN`, `FINWISE_LEDGER`; the default address is `127.0.0.1:8080`). It starts even when the snapshot file does not exist: the PIN works and reads answer `ledger_unavailable`. `GET /healthz` answers 200 without a session and says nothing about the ledger. Read and write timeouts are set, and `SIGTERM` shuts down gracefully. Serving the built interface from the binary is later work.

No dependency is added: everything here is in the standard library.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] For every `write` and `evaluate` method in the manifest, a POST with a valid session answers 403 with `{"error":{"kind":"read_only"}}`, including when the body is not valid JSON.
- [ ] For every route in the manifest except `session.status` and `session.unlock`, a POST without a session answers 401 `locked`.
- [ ] `POST /api/nope/nothing` answers 404 `unknown_method` as JSON; a GET on a method route answers `bad_request`.
- [ ] A correct unlock sets a cookie named `__Host-finwise-session` whose attributes are exactly `Path=/`, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` plus an expiry, with no `Domain`; with `--dev-insecure-cookie` the name has no prefix and `Secure` is absent.
- [ ] After three wrong PINs a fourth attempt with the right PIN is refused and `retryAfterSeconds` is between 1 and 300; after the clock advances 300 seconds the right PIN unlocks; a correct unlock after two wrong attempts resets the count.
- [ ] `session.status` reports `locked: true` without a cookie and `locked: false` with one.
- [ ] After `session.lock` the same cookie answers 401.
- [ ] A session unused for 12 hours answers 401; a request at 11 hours keeps it valid at 20 hours.
- [ ] `session.changePin` answers `read_only` and the PIN comparison function is not called.
- [ ] `finwise hash-pin` rejects `12345` and `abcdef`, and the string it prints for `123456` unlocks a server started with it; a server started with no hash, or with `not-a-hash`, exits non-zero.
- [ ] A POST with `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` answers 403; a POST with `Content-Type: text/plain` answers `bad_request`; a body over 1 MiB answers `bad_request`.
- [ ] A request carrying a sentinel string in its body, another as its PIN and a valid cookie produces log output containing none of the three.
- [ ] A test handler returning the reader's unsupported-version error answers 503 `ledger_unavailable`; one returning any other error answers 500 `internal`.
- [ ] The set of `read` methods in the manifest equals the registered handlers plus the pending list, and removing one name from the pending list makes that test fail.
- [ ] `finwise serve --listen 127.0.0.1:0 --ledger /nonexistent` starts, and `GET /healthz` answers 200.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` says how to run the backend.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and every row of the error table above has a test that produces it.

## Tests
- Unit: the hash format and its round trip; the lockout and the session expiry with an injected clock.
- Integration with `httptest`: the manifest-driven refusal of every write and evaluation; the session requirement on every route; the cookie's attributes; cross-origin, content type and size limits; the error mapping.
- Unit: the log line for a request with sentinels.
- Integration: the `serve` command started on a free port without a snapshot.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `cmd/finwise/`, `internal/api/`, `internal/contract/contract.go`, `internal/contract/contract_test.go`, `AGENTS.md`, `.gitignore`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `web/src/api/contract/session.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/index.ts`, `bin/ci`

title: Turn a ledger row into the transaction the app lists
description:
## What changes for the user
The bank's records are not the list a person expects to read. A card purchase and a bank debit carry opposite signs, a purchase abroad shows its price in another currency, the tax on it arrives as a separate row, paying the card bill looks like spending twice, and moving money into a savings pot looks like an expense. After this lands the app can turn those records into one line per purchase in reais, with the tax under its purchase, with transfers between the person's own accounts set apart, and with pot movements out of the general list. No record is ever dropped without being accounted for.

## Outcome
A Go package of pure functions, `internal/txrules`, that takes the rows the ledger reader returns for a period and gives back the transactions the app lists, each with its kind, signed amount in cents, Brazil day, counterpart and establishment key, plus a tally that places every input row in exactly one destination.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app over a SQLite ledger collected from the person's banks. A Go package, `internal/ledger`, already reads that ledger and returns rows faithfully, with amounts in integer cents and the raw provider fields parsed; it interprets nothing. This bead is the interpretation. It does no SQL and no I/O.

**The app's convention.** An amount is signed and negative means money out, on every kind of account. A day is `YYYY-MM-DD` in America/Sao_Paulo. The interface's contract for a transaction is `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`; its kinds and subtypes are the vocabulary this package maps to.

**Direction and sign.** The row's `type` (`DEBIT` or `CREDIT`) is only a direction, and the sign of the stored amount is inverted between account types: on a `BANK` account a debit is stored negative; on a `CREDIT` account (a card) a purchase is a positive debit and a payment or refund a negative credit. Direction comes from `type` together with the account type, never from the stored sign alone.

**Foreign purchases.** The stored amount is in the original currency. The value in reais is `raw.amountInAccountCurrency` when present. The app amount is the value in reais; the original amount and currency are kept for display.

**Day.** `date` is a UTC timestamp on every row; convert before taking the day. `creditCardMetadata.purchaseDate` exists on few rows, so `date` is the date.

**Kind.** Decided with the user: bank rows are split by payment method (PIX, boleto, and "Outros" for the rest: TED, TEF, debit, fees); card rows are those of `CREDIT` accounts. The kind is read from the account type, `raw.operationType` and `raw.paymentData.paymentMethod` together, because `operationType` alone lies: a bank row may be typed `OUTROS` and carry `paymentMethod` `PIX`. Vocabulary seen on bank accounts: `PIX`, `BOLETO`, `TED`, `TEF`, `CARTAO`, `FOLHA_PAGAMENTO`, `CONVENIO_ARRECADACAO`, `PACOTE_TARIFA_SERVICOS`, `ENCARGOS_JUROS_CHEQUE_ESPECIAL`, `TRANSFERENCIA_SALDO_RESERVADO`, `RESGATE_APLIC_FINANCEIRA`, `RENDIMENTO_APLIC_FINANCEIRA`, `OUTROS`; `paymentMethod` is one of `PIX`, `BOLETO`, `TED`, `TEF`, `OTHER` and exists only on bank rows. On card accounts: `PAGAMENTO`, `ESTORNO`, `TARIFA`, `PAGAMENTO_FATURA`, `OUTROS`, or none.

**Card rows typed `OUTROS`.** `operationType` cannot be the rule across banks: on C6 `OUTROS` is almost only tax, on Itaú it is everything the bank does not classify. Hiding only `PAGAMENTO_FATURA` would leave Itaú's bill payments counted as spending, and hiding `OUTROS` would drop real purchases. The groups, each row in exactly one:
- A tax row named after its purchase (C6): its amount is exactly 3.5% of a purchase with the same name on the same card within 3 days. It is attached to that purchase and leaves the list.
- An explicit tax row (Itaú): the description is `IOF INTERNACIONAL`. It is attached to the foreign purchase of the same day on the same card. The sources give no rule for a day with several foreign purchases: attach only when exactly one candidate exists, otherwise keep the row listed.
- A purchase abroad typed `OUTROS` (Itaú): an ordinary purchase.
- A bill payment seen from the card (Itaú): the description is `PAGAMENTO COM SALDO`. It is a movement.
- An early-payment discount: the description is `Desc Antecipa Parcelas`. The user confirmed it is a discount for paying instalments ahead; it is a credit under fees and interest.
- A credit with no keyword on the C6 card: the user confirmed these are refunds.
- A partial cancellation (Itaú): a refund. The sources give no keyword for it.

**Movements.** Listed, under their own kind, and never counted as an expense or as income by a caller: a bill payment (from the card side `PAGAMENTO_FATURA` or `PAGAMENTO COM SALDO`; the bank-account side has no written rule), and a transfer between the person's own accounts, recognised when the counterpart's document is one of the person's own in the ledger's `identities`. Savings-pot movements (`TRANSFERENCIA_SALDO_RESERVADO`, and Mercado Pago's `RESGATE_APLIC_FINANCEIRA` rows whose description starts with `Rendimentos`) leave the general list and are returned separately, per account, for the pot they belong to.

**Counterpart and establishment.** The ledger has no merchant on any row. A PIX or a boleto carries `paymentData.payer` and `.receiver`, each with a name and a document: the counterpart is the other party, its key is the document, and it is a person when the document has 11 digits and a company when it has 14. A card purchase has only its description: the display name comes from it and the key is the normalised text. Two descriptions that differ only in letter case, spacing or a trailing instalment marker such as `03/10` share a key. A document is another person's personal data: it is a key, it is never logged.

**What the sources leave open.** For each of these, write the smallest rule that is safe, state it in a comment, and report how many rows it matched on a real ledger, as a count only: the bank-account side of a bill payment; the keyword of a partial cancellation; the explicit tax row on a day with several foreign purchases; how far text normalisation goes. The safe default everywhere: a row no rule recognises stays in the list as an ordinary transaction of kind "Outros". Dropping it is the failure that matters.

**The tally.** Processing a period returns, beside the list, how many input rows were listed, attached to a purchase as tax, or returned as pot movements. Every input row id is in exactly one of the three.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A `BANK` debit of 50.00 yields -5000 and a `BANK` credit +5000; a `CREDIT`-account debit of 50.00 yields -5000 and a `CREDIT`-account credit +5000; each holds whichever sign the fixture stored.
- [ ] A purchase of 10.00 in USD with 55.00 in the account currency yields -5500 and keeps `1000` and `USD` as the original.
- [ ] A row dated `2026-03-01T02:30:00Z` has the day `2026-02-28`.
- [ ] A bank row typed `OUTROS` with `paymentMethod` `PIX` is a PIX.
- [ ] A row of 7.00 named like a purchase of 200.00 on the same card two days later is attached to it and absent from the list; the same row at 7.01, or four days later, or on another card, stays listed.
- [ ] `IOF INTERNACIONAL` on a day with exactly one foreign purchase on that card is attached; with two it stays listed.
- [ ] `PAGAMENTO_FATURA` and `PAGAMENTO COM SALDO` rows are movements; `Desc Antecipa Parcelas` is a positive fee credit; a keyword-less credit on a C6 card is a refund.
- [ ] A PIX out whose receiver's document is in `identities` is a movement between own accounts; the same PIX to another document is a PIX to a counterpart.
- [ ] `TRANSFERENCIA_SALDO_RESERVADO` rows and `RESGATE_APLIC_FINANCEIRA` rows starting with `Rendimentos` are absent from the list and present in the pot movements of their account.
- [ ] A PIX out names its receiver, is keyed by the receiver's document, and is a person for an 11-digit document and a company for a 14-digit one.
- [ ] `ACME STORE 03/10`, `acme  store` and `ACME STORE` share one establishment key.
- [ ] A row with an `operationType` no rule knows is listed as "Outros".
- [ ] For every fixture and for randomly generated inputs, each input row id is in exactly one of: listed, attached as tax, pot movement.
- [ ] The package imports neither `database/sql` nor `os`.
- [ ] A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs every month of a real snapshot through the rules and logs only counts: the tally, the rows per kind, and the rows matched by each rule left open above.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports a tally whose three parts sum to the number of input rows for every month.

## Tests
- Unit: one table-driven test per rule, each with rows that must match and rows that must not.
- Property: the tally invariant over generated inputs.
- Integration, opt-in: every month of a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each rule is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/txrules/`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/rules.ts`, `bin/ci`

One new package of pure functions and its tests. If a rule needs a raw field the reader does not parse yet, that field is added to the reader's row type with its test and nothing else in `internal/ledger` changes.
close_reason: internal/txrules turns the reader's rows into the transactions the app lists: direction from type and account type, foreign purchases in reais with the original kept, the Brazil day, kinds read from operationType and paymentMethod together, card rows sorted by their own text and direction, movements, pot movements set apart, counterpart and establishment key, and a tally that places every input row in exactly one destination. bin/ci: CI green. The tally invariant holds over fixtures and over random inputs, and the opt-in run over a real snapshot balanced every month. Rules written where the sources were silent, each stated in a comment beside the code: the bank side of a bill payment by its text; a card credit with no operation type that names a payment is a bill payment; refund stems for a cancellation; an explicit tax row attaches only when exactly one foreign purchase exists on that card that day; text normalisation stops at case, accents, spacing and a trailing instalment marker. A tax row is paired only within the rows given, so a caller reads the days around its period.

title: Open every screen on the backend's recorded answers
description:
## What changes for the user
The backend and the screens are written in two languages by different hands, and each is tested against its own idea of the other. A field the backend names slightly differently, or leaves out, would pass both sides' tests and show up as a blank on the person's screen. After this lands every screen is also opened, in the gate, against the exact answers the real backend gives, so that kind of mismatch is caught before anyone sees it.

## Outcome
A test in the interface's suite serves the backend's recorded answers through the API contract and mounts every screen over them, for a ledger with every shape and for an empty one.

## Context
finwise's Go backend records what each of its `read` methods answers over two invented ledgers, as golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/<ledger>/<domain>.<method>.json`; a Go test keeps those files equal to what the handlers return, and they are generated only from invented data. The interface (`web/`) reaches a backend through the `FinwiseApi` contract and already has a sweep test that mounts every route over two states of its in-memory stand-in and fails on a thrown error, an unhandled rejection, or `NaN`, `undefined`, `Infinity`, `null` or `Invalid Date` in the rendered text.

The two sides agree on shape through a JSON Schema generated from the contract, and the Go answers are validated against it. A schema cannot say whether a screen holds on those answers. This bead closes that gap by reusing both existing pieces: the golden files as data, the sweep as the assertion.

**The replay API.** A test helper builds a `FinwiseApi` whose `read` methods answer from the golden files of one ledger and whose other methods reject with the contract's `read_only` error, as the backend does. A method whose arguments select among answers (a month, an id) answers from the file recorded for those arguments; the helper fails loudly when asked for something that was not recorded, so a screen that requests an unexpected month is a finding and not a silent `undefined`. The session methods answer unlocked.

**Where the files are read from.** The golden directory belongs to the Go side and stays there; the test reads it by path from the repository root. It is not copied into `web/`, because a copy can go stale.

**Two implementations, one first day.** The interface's in-memory stand-in and the Go backend each say what an empty ledger looks like, and nothing keeps them saying the same thing: a group label, a default threshold or the shape of an empty budget can drift on one side and every test of both sides still passes. Over the empty ledger there is no bank data to differ, so the two must agree exactly. A test compares, for every `read` method, the backend's recorded answer over its empty ledger with the stand-in's answer over its empty-ledger state, deep-equal, apart from a short written list of fields that legitimately differ (the clock's day, the wording of the sync state) with the reason for each. A difference outside that list is fixed on the side that departed from the contract's intent, and never by adding to the list without a reason.

**What a failure means.** A screen breaking over a golden answer is a real mismatch between the two sides. It is fixed where the fault is: in the handler when the answer departs from the contract's intent, in the screen when the screen assumed more than the contract promises. It is never fixed by editing a golden file by hand.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The replay helper answers every `read` method of the manifest from a golden file, for both recorded ledgers, and a missing file for a `read` method fails the test by name.
- [ ] The sweep mounts every route of `web/src/router.ts`, plus the transaction panel, a pot's page, an account's page, the card page and a subscription's page where the ledger has one, over both ledgers, with the same assertions as the existing sweep.
- [ ] A request for arguments that were not recorded fails the test with the method and the arguments in the message.
- [ ] A write through the replay API rejects with `read_only`.
- [ ] For every `read` method, the backend's recorded answer over the empty ledger equals the stand-in's answer over its empty-ledger state, apart from a written list of excepted fields, each with its reason; changing one label in either side makes the test fail and name the method and the field.
- [ ] Renaming a field in one golden file makes the sweep fail on the screen that reads it.
- [ ] The test runs inside `npm --prefix web test`, and so inside `bin/ci`, with no browser and no running backend.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the sweep passes over both recorded ledgers.

## Tests
- Component: the sweep over every route and both recorded ledgers.
- Unit: the replay helper's coverage of the manifest, its refusal of writes, and its failure on unrecorded arguments.
- The guard is broken once on purpose, by renaming a field in a golden file, and the failing screen named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/test/`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/router.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `bin/ci`

One test helper and one test file. If the sweep finds a mismatch, the fix lands in the handler or the screen at fault, in the same pull request, with a test beside it.

title: Answer the frame, the accounts and the transactions from the ledger
description:
## What changes for the user
Until now every amount on screen is invented. After this lands, a person who starts the backend against their own ledger and unlocks with the PIN sees their real accounts and their real transactions: the right month, one line per purchase in reais, the tax under the purchase it belongs to, transfers between their own accounts set apart. What the app does not know yet (which budget line a purchase belongs to, tags, nicknames) shows as not filled in, never as a guess.

## Outcome
The backend answers six methods of the interface's contract from the ledger: `shell.overview`, `accounts.list`, `accounts.detail`, `transactions.list`, `transactions.filterOptions` and `transactions.detail`. Every answer is checked against the contract's schema, recorded as a golden file from invented data, and money leaves the server as an exact decimal.

## Context
finwise's interface talks to its backend through a contract described for Go by `internal/contract/contract.json`: for each method a route, a class, and schemas for its arguments and result. The HTTP layer (`internal/api`) already dispatches a `read` method to a handler registered for it, behind the PIN, and keeps a test-side list of reads still without a handler. The ledger reader (`internal/ledger`) returns typed rows in integer cents; `internal/txrules` turns a period's rows into the app's transactions (kind, signed amount, Brazil day, counterpart, establishment key, tax attached to its purchase, movements, pot movements set apart) with a tally that places every row. This bead joins them and is the first to show real data.

**What the rules expect of their caller.** `txrules.Interpret(rows, reference)` takes the reader's rows plus the accounts and the person's own documents, and returns the listed transactions, the tax rows it attached, the pot movements per account and the tally. Four things follow for this bead:
- A tax row is paired only with a purchase among the rows it was given, and a tax can fall up to 3 days from its purchase. Interpreting exactly one month would leave a tax listed on its own when the purchase is in the neighbouring month. Read the period widened by 3 days on each side, interpret, then keep the transactions whose day is inside the period. The month's tally is checked on the widened read; the cut to the period is checked by a test with a purchase on the last day of a month and its tax on the first day of the next.
- A movement (a bill payment, a transfer between own accounts) keeps one of the contract's kinds and carries a `Movement` field; it is not a separate kind.
- An attached tax is already inside its purchase's `Amount` and is also in `Tax`; it is never added a second time.
- A foreign row with no value in reais is flagged `Unconverted` and its amount is not in reais. It must not enter any sum, and the opt-in run over a real ledger reports how many there are.

**What is real and what is empty.** The backend is read-only and has no database of its own yet, so anything only the person can author comes back as on a fresh install. The contract was widened for that beforehand: a field with no honest value on a fresh install is nullable. The rule here is the same: a figure the ledger supports is real; anything else is the contract's empty value; nothing is invented.

| method | from the ledger | empty for now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `shell.overview` | today (the server's clock in America/Sao_Paulo), the first month with a transaction, the current month as the last, the sync state | pending count 0, closed months `[]` |
| `accounts.list`, `accounts.detail` | every current account with its balance, its bank, whether it has been idle for more than 30 days, and an account's transactions | the bucket an account belongs to |
| `transactions.list` | the clean list for the query's period through `internal/txrules`, newest first, filtered as the query asks | budget line, who classified it, confidence, tags, nickname, exclusion, split, reimbursement |
| `transactions.filterOptions` | the accounts | tags `[]`, lines `[]` |
| `transactions.detail` | the same base fields, the tax attached to the purchase, the original amount and currency, the instalment, the bill | history `[]`, notes, every section the person fills; `null` for an unknown id |

With an empty ledger (no account, no transaction) the first and last month are both the current month and every list is empty.

**The sync state.** `shell.overview.sync` is `ok` with the day and time of the last complete run, or a warning with a message when a connection is in trouble (a status other than `UPDATED`, an execution status other than `SUCCESS`, a last update older than 48 hours, or a consent about to expire). A message the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in one Go file with every other such string; everything else in the code is English. The stand-in's wording in `web/src/api/fake/` is the reference.

**Money on the wire.** The contract carries money as a JSON number in reais with decimals, negative meaning money out. The server holds integer cents. The conversion happens once, in a type whose JSON encoding writes the cents as a decimal literal with two places, so no float arithmetic ever touches an amount. `1999` is written `19.99` and `-6510` is written `-65.10`.

**No total of the month is computed here.** The contract's "spent" figures (the home summary's limit, the weekly review) mean what was spent on the budget's variable lines, and no transaction has a budget line yet, so those figures are 0 in later work and this bead adds no sum over the list.

**Conformance.** A test runs every handler of this bead over two ledgers built by the reader's fixture builder, one with every shape the rules know and one empty, and validates each answer against the method's result schema in the manifest with `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6`, a test-only dependency. The same answers are stored as golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/<ledger>/<domain>.<method>.json`; the test fails when an answer differs from its file, and `-update` rewrites them. Because a golden file is committed to a public repository, `-update` refuses to run when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set.

**A real ledger.** A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs every handler over that file for every month it holds, validates every answer against its schema, checks that the tally of each month sums to its input rows, and logs counts only. No value from a real ledger is ever printed, logged or committed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the six methods answers 200 with a valid session, and its answer validates against its result schema over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] Renaming one JSON field of any answer type makes the conformance test fail.
- [ ] `transactions.list` for February 2026 includes a fixture row dated `2026-03-01T02:30:00Z` and its list for March does not.
- [ ] A fixture purchase with its tax row appears as one line whose detail carries the tax; the tax row has no line of its own.
- [ ] A fixture pot movement is absent from `transactions.list`; a transfer between own accounts is present with the movement kind.
- [ ] Over the empty ledger, `shell.overview` gives the current month as first and last, and every list method answers `[]`.
- [ ] `transactions.detail` answers `null` for an unknown id.
- [ ] A purchase on the last day of a month whose tax row is dated the first day of the next appears in the first month as one line carrying the tax, and the tax row appears in neither month.
- [ ] A snapshot file that exists but is not a SQLite database answers 503 `ledger_unavailable`: the reader returns a typed error for a snapshot it cannot read, and the HTTP layer maps it. Today that case answers `internal`.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` no longer says that no backend exists, and says how to see real data at the desktop.
- [ ] `1999` cents is encoded as `19.99`, `-6510` as `-65.10`, `0` as `0.00`; no handler converts cents to a float.
- [ ] A fixture connection with a status other than `UPDATED` produces a sync warning whose message is in Portuguese.
- [ ] Running the golden test with `-update` and `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` set fails without writing a file.
- [ ] The pending list of reads without a handler no longer names these six methods.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer of every month and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` and no other direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports every month's tally summing to its input rows with every answer valid.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the money encoding; the sync warning; the query's filters and ordering; the cut of a widened read back to its period.
- Integration with `httptest`: each method through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`, `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `go.mod`, `go.sum`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `internal/txrules/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler, wire-type and test files in the existing HTTP package, its golden directory, and one test dependency. If a handler needs a ledger query that does not exist, it is added to `internal/ledger` as a new file with its test.
close_reason: The backend answers shell.overview, accounts.list, accounts.detail, transactions.list, transactions.filterOptions and transactions.detail from the ledger. Money is written from integer cents as a decimal with two places and a test forbids floats in the HTTP layer. A month is read three days wider and cut back, so a tax and its purchase across a month's end are one line. Every answer validates against its schema in the manifest over two fixture ledgers and is recorded as a golden file from invented data; the golden update refuses to run with a real snapshot set. A snapshot that is not a database answers ledger_unavailable. bin/ci: CI green. Over a real snapshot every answer of every month validated, every month's tally summed to its input, and every account was placed in exactly one bank; the built server was also called end to end against it. One departure from the bead: a bank account's bucket is a required field of the contract and is answered as available.

title: A refused month close folds the step it was started from
description:
## What changes for the user
In the monthly closing, pressing "Fechar o mês" while the app cannot save shows the message that nothing was changed, and the month does stay open. But the step the person was looking at folds shut, as if something had happened. After this lands a refused close leaves the screen exactly as it was before the click: the step stays open.

## Outcome
A refused or failed close of a month leaves the closing tab's open step open.

## Context
finwise's interface runs against a backend that is read-only for now: every write answers with a `read_only` error, and one central function turns that into a toast ("Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.") and a bump of the revision counter so the screens fetch again. No write call site catches errors itself, on purpose.

The closing tab, `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`, keeps which step is unfolded in its view store. Its `askToClose` sets `view.openStep = -1` before it calls the write that closes the month, so the step folds whether or not the write succeeds. Every other write on the screens changes local state only after the server answered, or not at all; this is the one place found where local state moves first.

The fix belongs in the screen: fold the step only once the close has succeeded. The central failure handling is not changed, and no error is caught here.

A test helper already exists for this kind of check: `web/src/test/readOnly.ts` wraps the stand-in so that every write is refused the way the backend refuses it, and `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts` already refuses a month close through a mounted screen and asserts the toast and the open month.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Mount the Revisão closing tab on the stand-in wrapped by the read-only helper, on an open month.
2. Unfold the last step, "Fechar o mês", and confirm closing the month.
3. Observed: the read-only toast appears and the month is still open, but the step is folded.
4. Expected: the read-only toast appears, the month is still open, and the step is still unfolded.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After a refused "Fechar o mês" through the mounted closing tab, the step that was unfolded is still unfolded.
- [ ] After a successful close on the plain stand-in the step folds, as today.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the regression test fails when the fold is moved back before the write.

## Tests
- Component, regression: a refused close through the mounted closing tab leaves the step unfolded.
- Component: a successful close folds it.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`, `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `web/src/screens/revisao/useClosingActions.ts`, `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `bin/ci`

title: Answer a pot's yield fast and open the month into its daily rows
description:
## What changes for the user
Against a real ledger the Cofrinhos screen, a pot's page and the Patrimônio screen each take about fifteen seconds to open, while every other screen opens at once. And on a pot's page the month's yield is one figure, where the person asked for it to open into the days behind it; that list is always empty. After this lands the three screens open as fast as the others, and the month's yield opens into its daily rows, with a day the bank's records cannot support shown as unknown rather than as zero.

## Outcome
Every yield figure the backend answers (the pots list, a pot's page, the net worth) comes from one fast computation over the balance history, which also gives the daily rows of a pot's month. The collector's own yield statement stays in the reader only as the reference the new computation is tested against.

## Context
finwise's read-only Go backend answers the pots and the net worth from the ledger a collector fills every night. The contract's pot detail carries the month's yield and `days`, the rows behind it; the user decided in the feature interview that yield is shown per month and opens to its daily rows.

Yield is not the change in balance: a deposit raises the balance and yields nothing. The collector's README has a statement for it, copied into the reader (`internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`) and run as three statements over the same CTEs because the single statement does not prepare in this module's SQLite. It answers **one figure per window** between two days, with a `reason` column that says when the figure cannot be computed. The balance history is one sighting per night.

**Measured over a real ledger, by the review, three runs each on the built server:** `savingsPots.list` 12.5 to 15.1 s, `savingsPots.detail` 14.7 s, `netWorth.overview` 13.7 to 15.3 s. Every other read answered in under 0.4 s, including `home.summary`, which reads the same pots and balances without asking for a yield. The handlers already ask the statement only once per account that has a pot to follow, twice in all on that ledger, so the cost is the statement itself, about seven seconds a call, not the number of calls.

That statement is also why the daily rows are empty: a row per day means a window per pair of consecutive sightings, and asking it once per pair took about 70 seconds.

The reader already has a fast read of every sighting's balances and pots (`internal/ledger/history.go`), which the net worth's chart uses. `internal/potrules` already has what turns rows into a month: `DayYield`, and `YieldOfMonth`, which sums a pot's rows, keeps them oldest first, and makes the month unknown when any row is.

What is missing is the yield of each pair of consecutive sightings computed without the collector's statement: from the sightings' balances and the transfers between them, in Go or in one set-based statement, with the same formula and the same reasons for "cannot be computed" as the collector's statement gives for that pair. The collector's statement stays as the reference: a test runs both over fixture ledgers and requires the new rows to equal the reference's answer for every pair, including the pairs with a deposit, a withdrawal, a pending transfer, a pot that appears, and a pot that closes. No handler runs the collector's statement at request time.

A wall-clock figure is not something the work can honestly produce on a shared machine; the absence of the slow statement from the request path is, and a test asserts it. The review measures the time.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `savingsPots.detail` answers one daily row per pair of consecutive sightings of the month for a pot with a stable identity, oldest first, each with its day and its yield or unknown.
- [ ] When every daily row of a month is known, their sum equals the month's yield to the cent; when any is unknown, the month's yield is unknown.
- [ ] For every pair of consecutive sightings in the fixture ledgers, the new row equals what the collector's statement answers for that pair, figure and reason.
- [ ] A day with a deposit and no yield is a row of zero, not the deposit.
- [ ] A pot without a stable identity has no daily rows and an unknown yield.
- [ ] `savingsPots.list`, `savingsPots.detail` and `netWorth.overview` take their yield figures from the new computation, and a test fails if any read handler runs the collector's yield statement.
- [ ] The golden files of the three methods are re-recorded from the fixture ledgers, and the only differences from before are the daily rows that used to be empty.
- [ ] Any new statement lives in the reader's registry and is prepared against the collector's real schema by the existing test.
- [ ] The time each of the three reads takes over a real ledger is measured **by the review**, not by the lane, three runs each on a quiet machine, against the figures above, and recorded on the pull request; each is expected under one second.
- [ ] A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set compares the new rows with the collector's statement over a sample of at least 20 pairs of a real ledger and logs counts only: pairs compared, equal, unknown.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports every sampled pair equal.

## Tests
- Unit over fixture ledgers: the new rows against the collector's statement, pair by pair.
- Unit: the daily rows of a month, their order, their sum against the month's figure, unknown days.
- Golden: the answers of the three methods.
- Unit: no read handler reaches the collector's yield statement.
- Integration, opt-in: a sample of pairs of a real ledger, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/api/pots.go`, `internal/api/pots_yield.go`, `internal/api/pots_detail.go`, `internal/api/net_worth.go`, `internal/api/pots_test.go`, `internal/api/net_worth_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/contract/savings-pots.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/net-worth.ts`, `bin/ci`

The yield of a pair of sightings gets a second, fast implementation beside the reference one, and the three handlers that show a yield switch to it. The card, the home summary and every other read are not touched.
